questions.question: Consider the max-flow problem of a directed network with a source node $s$ and the sink node $t$. Let $x_{ij}$ (respectively, $x_{ji}$) denote the amount of positive flow from node $i$ to node $j$ (respectively, from node $j$ to node $i$). Write the node balanced equations of a nodes $i$ and $j$ where $i,j \ne s$ and $i,j \ne t$. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
For an intermediate node (not $s$, not $t$) the flow in equals the flow out.
Node $i$: $$\sum_{k} x_{ik} - \sum_{k} x_{ki} = 0, \qquad i \ne s, t$$
Node $j$: $$\sum_{k} x_{jk} - \sum_{k} x_{kj} = 0, \qquad j \ne s, t$$
($x_{ik}$: flow leaving $i$ along $(i,k)$; $x_{ki}$: flow entering $i$. The arc between them appears as $x_{ij}$ in both equations, as outflow of $i$ and inflow of $j$, and $x_{ji}$ the other way.) Equivalently, with net flow $f(i,k) = x_{ik} - x_{ki}$: $\sum_k f(i,k) = 0$.

rubric.point: Node $j$: the same balance written for $j$

questions.question:
(b) Answer the following questions
(i) An Augmenting Path in the Ford Fulkerson algorithm. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
An augmenting path $P$ is a simple directed path from the source $s$ to the sink $t$ in the residual network $G_x$, i.e. every arc on it still has positive residual capacity $r_{ij} > 0$. Its capacity is the bottleneck
$$\delta(P) = \min_{(i,j) \in P} r_{ij},$$
and the flow from $s$ to $t$ can be increased by $\delta(P)$ by sending that much along every arc of $P$ (then $r_{ij} \leftarrow r_{ij} - \delta(P)$, $r_{ji} \leftarrow r_{ji} + \delta(P)$). Ford–Fulkerson stops when no augmenting path exists; the flow is then maximum.

rubric.point: A directed path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual network (every arc has positive residual capacity)
Its capacity is the bottleneck $\delta(P) = \min r_{ij}$, by which the flow is increased

questions.question:
(b) Answer the following questions
(ii) Explain what do you mean by the residual network in the Ford-Fulkersonalgorithm. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Given a feasible flow $x$ with capacities $u_{ij}$, the residual network $G_x = (V, E_x)$ has the same nodes, and each arc $(i,j)$ of the network is replaced by two arcs:
• forward arc $(i,j)$ with residual capacity $r_{ij} = u_{ij} - x_{ij}$ (how much more flow can still be sent from $i$ to $j$);
• backward arc $(j,i)$ with residual capacity $r_{ji} = x_{ij}$ (how much of the existing flow can be cancelled by sending it back).
$E_x$ keeps only the arcs with $r_{ij} > 0$. So the residual network shows where extra flow can still be pushed (or undone), and augmenting paths are searched for in it.

rubric.point: Forward residual capacity $r_{ij} = u_{ij} - x_{ij}$: remaining capacity
Backward arc with $r_{ji} = x_{ij}$ (flow can be cancelled); only arcs with positive residual capacity are kept

questions.question: Establish the connection between the minimum cost network flow problem and theshortest path problem. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
The shortest path problem is a special case of the minimum cost network flow problem.
Min-cost flow: $\min \sum_{(i,j)} c_{ij} x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} = b_i$ for every node $i$, $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$.
Take the arc costs $c_{ij}$ to be the distances, give the source a supply of one unit ($b_s = 1$), the sink a demand of one unit ($b_t = -1$), every other node $b_i = 0$ (what comes in goes out), and capacities $u_{ij} = 1$. Then the cheapest way to send one unit of flow from $s$ to $t$ is along the shortest $s$–$t$ path: $x_{ij} = 1$ exactly on the arcs of that path, and the minimum cost equals the shortest path length. (The LP is integral, so the flows come out 0 or 1 without forcing them.)

rubric.point: Costs = distances; supply 1 at $s$, demand 1 at $t$ ($b_t = -1$), $b_i = 0$ elsewhere (capacities 1)
The min-cost flow then sends one unit along the shortest $s$–$t$ path; its cost is the shortest distance

questions.question: Construct a directed graph with $s$ and $t$ as the source and terminal node, respectively, and define an $(s - t)$ cut-$(A,B)$. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Example network (capacities on the arcs): $s \to a$ (4), $s \to b$ (3), $a \to b$ (2), $b \to a$ (1), $a \to t$ (3), $b \to t$ (5).
An $s$–$t$ cut $(A, B)$ is a partition of the node set $V$ into two disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ ($A \cup B = V$, $A \cap B = \emptyset$) with $s \in A$ and $t \in B$. The arcs from $A$ to $B$ form the cut set: removing them leaves no directed path from $s$ to $t$. Example: $A = \{s, a\}$, $B = \{b, t\}$, cut set $\{(s,b), (a,b), (a,t)\}$.
(Its capacity is the sum over arcs from $A$ to $B$ only: $3 + 2 + 3 = 8$; the arc $b \to a$ is not counted.)

rubric.point: A directed network with $s$ and $t$ drawn/listed
Cut defined as a partition $(A, B)$ of the nodes, disjoint, $s \in A$, $t \in B$ (arcs from $A$ to $B$ disconnect $t$ from $s$)

questions.question: Which constraint in the mathematical model of the minimum spanning tree problemensures that the graph is a tree graph. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
MST model ($x_e = 1$ if edge $e$ is in the tree):
$$\min \sum_{e \in E} c_e x_e \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{e \in \delta(S)} x_e \ge 1 \ \ \forall S \subset V, S \ne \emptyset; \qquad \sum_{e \in E} x_e = n - 1; \qquad x_e \in \{0, 1\}.$$
The tree constraint is $$\sum_{e \in E} x_e = n - 1,$$ the "tree property": a tree on $n$ vertices has exactly $n - 1$ edges. Together with the cut (connectivity) constraints, which force the chosen edges to connect every set $S$ to the rest of the graph, a connected subgraph with $n - 1$ edges cannot contain a cycle, so it is a spanning tree.

rubric.point: Names $\sum_{e \in E} x_e = n - 1$ as the tree constraint
Explains: a connected graph (from $\sum_{e \in \delta(S)} x_e \ge 1$) with $n-1$ edges has no cycle, so it is a tree

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf p. 9 (2021 Test), which marks $\sum x_e = n - 1$ as the "tree property". Course notes: MST model, DisCopt.pdf PDF p. 14 (eqs. 21–25: "(23) ensures that the spanning tree is connected, while the number of edges requirement is fulfilled by (24)").
questions.keyDispute: The notes say (23) gives connectivity and (24), $\sum x_e = n-1$, the edge count; neither alone makes a tree. If the marker wants one constraint, give $\sum x_e = n - 1$ and say it works together with the connectivity constraints.

questions.question: Describe the difference between the Hamiltonian and the Eulerian cycle in graphtheory. Use an example graph for each concept. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start (it need not use every edge).
Eulerian cycle: a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start (vertices may be visited several times). An undirected connected graph has one if and only if every vertex has even degree.
So the difference is vertices versus edges: Hamiltonian = each vertex once, Eulerian = each edge once. (The TSP looks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle.)
Example 1 (Hamiltonian, not Eulerian): square 1–2–5–4–1 with a centre vertex 3 joined to 1, 2, 4, 5. The cycle 1–2–3–5–4–1 visits every vertex once. It is not Eulerian: vertices 1, 2, 4, 5 have odd degree 3.
Example 2 (Eulerian, not Hamiltonian): a "bow-tie", two triangles 1–3–4 and 2–3–5 sharing vertex 3. The closed walk 1–3–2–5–3–4–1 uses all 6 edges once (degrees 2, 2, 4, 2, 2 are all even). It is not Hamiltonian: any cycle through all vertices must pass through 3 twice.

rubric.point: Hamiltonian cycle: visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start
Eulerian cycle: uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start
A correct example graph for each, with the cycle shown

questions.question: Give an example of a sub-tour that can occur for the 7-city asymmetric TSP? Howdoes the sub-tour elimination constraint of ATSP differ from the same constraint of the symmetric travelling salesman problem (STSP)? Why? [2 + 1 + 2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Example sub-tour for 7 cities (directed): $1 \to 2 \to 1$ and $3 \to 4 \to 5 \to 6 \to 7 \to 3$. Every city has exactly one arc in and one arc out, so the assignment constraints $\sum_i x_{ij} = 1$ and $\sum_j x_{ij} = 1$ hold, but the route is two separate cycles, not one tour. It violates the subtour constraint for $S = \{1, 2\}$: $x_{12} + x_{21} = 2 > |S| - 1 = 1$.
ATSP subtour elimination constraints ($x_{ij} = 1$ if the salesman goes directly from city $i$ to city $j$):
$$\sum_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S,\ j \ne i} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1, \qquad \forall S \subset V,\ 2 \le |S| \le n - 2.$$
For any proper subset $S$ of cities, the arcs used inside $S$ must be fewer than $|S|$, so they cannot close a cycle on $S$ alone.
STSP subtour elimination constraints ($x_e = 1$ if undirected edge $e$ is in the tour, $E(S)$ = edges with both ends in $S$):
$$\sum_{e \in E(S)} x_e \le |S| - 1, \qquad \forall S \subset V,\ 3 \le |S| \le n - 3.$$
Why the ranges differ: in the ATSP the arcs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ are different, so two cities can form a sub-tour $i \to j \to i$; sets with $|S| = 2$ must be included. In the STSP $\{i, j\}$ is a single edge that can be used at most once, so a sub-tour needs at least 3 cities and $|S| = 2$ is not needed. The upper limit comes from the complement: if $S$ holds a sub-tour then so does $V \setminus S$, which needs at least 2 cities (ATSP, so $|S| \le n - 2$) or at least 3 cities (STSP, so $|S| \le n - 3$). The ATSP version also sums over ordered pairs $i \ne j$ instead of undirected edges.

rubric.point: A valid directed sub-tour example on 7 cities (separate cycles, each city one arc in and one out)
Difference stated: ATSP sums $x_{ij}$ over ordered pairs in $S$ with $2 \le |S| \le n-2$; STSP sums $x_e$ over $E(S)$ with $3 \le |S| \le n-3$
Why: directed arcs allow a 2-city sub-tour $i \to j \to i$
Why: an undirected edge is used at most once, so STSP sub-tours need ≥ 3 cities (and the complement bounds the upper limit)
